To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

California rangeland and natural area land managers and restoration practitioners face a wide range of weed species, have varying weed management goals and practices, and face similar barriers to weed management implementation across bioregions and management practices.

weed management practices vary regionally in effectiveness and adoption but herbicide use is most commonly used and most effective; however, herbicide use faces considerable challenges including nonteget impacts, cost, and perceived effectiveness, which may be mitigated by improved training and outreach; and that grazing for weed management faces challenges related to effectiveness, cost and public perception, which may be improved through improved training and outreach.

weed management practices vary across regions, herbicide use is the most highly rated tool for weed management, and barriers to implementation of practices include operational challenges, potential adverse impacts, perceived ineffectiveness, and public perception.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a science-based approach to weed management on California's rangelands and other natural areas, and we believe that the results of this study will be of great use to practitioners and land managers in California and beyond.
the development and implementation of management practices to control invasive and weedy plant species on California's working rangelands and other natural areas.
understanding how practitioners perceive the effectiveness of management practices and barriers to implementation, and the potential for management science to address these issues.
